newsitem.title: UK: Copper, aluminum price forecasts revised up - EIU.
newsitem.headline: Copper, aluminum price forecasts revised up - EIU.

text.p: Copper prices are seen higher than previously forecast in 1997, reflecting a smaller than expected projected surplus, the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) said in a report.
The EIU also revised up price forecasts for aluminium, while lead, nickel and zinc price forecasts have been revised down in the EIU's first quarter 1997 commodities report.
Three months copper prices were forecast to average 102.5 cents per pound ($2,260 per tonne) in 1997, decreasing to 95.0 cents ($2,094) in 1998.
"Higher demand in the fourth quarter of 1996 suggests that consumption is growing more rapidly than expected, but the surplus will probably be absorbed by stockbuilding in China," the report said.
In aluminium, prices were projected at $1,588 per tonne in 1997 and $1,550 in 1998.
"Low prices have caused producers to delay restarts. This, combined with a pick-up in consumption growth, means the market will be in deficit in 1997," the report said.
The lead market's 1997 deficit has been revised downwards, although stocks are expected to fall to less than four week's consumption by the end of the year.
In 1998 the EIU expects the lead market to move into surplus as Western consumption slows and non-Western metal exports remain high.
Prices were forecast at 36.0 cents per pound ($794) this year and 34.0 cents ($749) in 1998.
The nickel market is expected to return to surplus this year despite a recovering in stainless steel output.
Nickel prices were seen at $3.45 per pound ($7,605) on average in 1997 and $3.38 ($7,452) in 1998.
Tin prices are expected to hit $2.95 per pound ($6,503) this year on good market fundamentals, although higher sales on Chinese metal into Western markets, which will limit further price gains.
On average tin prices are forecast at $2.84 per pound ($6,261) in 1997 and $3.13 ($6,900) in 1998.

Zinc prices are seen rising by 15 percent this year, although the market's deficit will narrow this year and next on weakening consumption and continued high exports of metals from non-Western countries.
In 1997 zinc is projected to average 53 cents per pound ($1,168), rising to 55.5 cents ($1,224) in 1998.
